items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists reprogram immune cells inside the body to fight cancer
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a way to create cancer-fighting CAR-T cells directly inside the body, potentially avoiding the slow and extremely expensive process of removing, engineering, and reinfusing a patient’s immune cells. Using a two-particle delivery system, the researchers sent CRISPR gene-editing tools and new cancer-targeting DNA specifically into T cells, where the DNA was inserted at a precise location in the genome.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
items.content_html: Scientists discovered that disrupting the chemical messages bacteria use to communicate can push dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance. The approach could lead to new treatments for gum disease that control harmful bacteria without destroying beneficial species.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
items.content_html: A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, suggests that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own evolutionary patterns.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

New research suggests animals could have evolved as early as 800 to 700 million years ago, roughly 200 million years earlier than some previous estimates. If so, the first animals may have lived before or during Snowball Earth, leaving behind little trace because their soft bodies were rarely preserved.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
items.content_html: Ancient pottery from Tampa Bay appears to have been made by migrant craftspeople who brought specialized Mississippian pottery-making knowledge hundreds of miles south. Remarkably, they even incorporated crushed fragments of older homeland pottery into new vessels, preserving a physical link to their past across generations.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
items.content_html: Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid.

items.title: [reddit.com] Physicist Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize for Antarctic neutrino observatory
items.content_html: Belgian-born physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded him 12 million Swedish kronor; the prize ceremony is scheduled for Dec. 10 [npr.org#2][physicsworld.com#1][nationalheraldindia.com#1]. Halzen proposed using South Pole ice to detect neutrinos in 1988. Completed in 2011, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors embedded in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice to record flashes produced when neutrinos collide with atoms. It detected the first high-energy neutrinos from beyond the solar system in 2013. Later observations identified a distant blazar as a source and detected neutrinos from within the Milky Way [theguardian.com#1][newscientist.com#1][astronomy.com#1]. Neutrinos can travel to Earth from distant, energetic environments while preserving information about their origins [bbc.co.uk#1][theguardian.com#1]. Halzen said he is working on a new proposal and hopes the Nobel recognition will help secure its approval [abcnews.com#1].

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists finally see how nature moves energy so efficiently
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have captured key steps in a chemical reaction that helps nature transfer energy with remarkable efficiency. Ultrafast X-rays revealed how changes involving electrons and protons are closely linked to the rearrangement of surrounding water molecules. Because similar reactions drive photosynthesis and other energy-conversion processes, the technique could help scientists develop better catalysts, fuel cells, and flow batteries.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A new kind of magnetism could unlock faster, more efficient computers
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered evidence of altermagnetism in a thin, highly tunable material that could help electronics use electron spin instead of relying only on electrical charge. The unusual magnetic state may enable faster, more energy-efficient devices without the unwanted magnetic interference caused by conventional magnets.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a human brain gene that can jump through DNA
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Scientists have discovered a human gene with a remarkable double life: it appears to play an important role in brain cells while still retaining the ability to jump around the genome. Called BC200, the gene evolved millions of years ago from a mobile piece of DNA known as a transposon, but unlike most genes that arose this way, it never lost its mobility. Researchers even found BC200 embedded inside a human poxvirus, suggesting it may have jumped from infected skin cells into the virus.

items.title: [phys.org] Forensic study finds signs of sacrifice in ancient Egyptian royal burials
items.content_html: A forensic re-examination of 46 skulls excavated near First Dynasty royal tombs at Umm el-Qaab, Egypt, identified potentially fatal injuries in 18, strengthening the case that some people buried there were killed as retainers after a ruler’s death [sciencealert.com#1][theguardian.com#1][thenationalnews.com#1]. The skulls came from burials around the tombs of King Djer, King Djet and Queen Merneith; many graves were associated with royal officials and artisans [theguardian.com#1][skai.gr#1]. British Egyptologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s and suspected retainer sacrifice, but could not identify fatal injuries. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University interpreted the newly identified trauma as evidence that at least some people died violently, but stressed that the sample is small and cannot establish what happened to everyone buried there [theguardian.com#1][arstechnica.com#1]. Petrie reburied most of the remains, and Campbell said she would like to locate and analyze them [popsci.com#1][sciencealert.com#1].

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The “glue” holding your cells together has a surprising second job
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered that E-cadherin, a protein best known as the “glue” holding cells and tissues together, has a surprising second job: helping epithelial cells swallow nearby dead cells. Using live zebrafish and mouse embryos, researchers found that cells can dramatically reshape their lower surfaces to engulf cellular debris while keeping their upper surfaces stable, allowing protective barriers to remain sealed.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
items.content_html:
🌾 🔧 🔭 ✏️

Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] MEGATRON simulations link JWST galaxies with ancient stellar clues
items.content_html: Researchers in the MEGATRON project have published four studies using detailed simulations to trace how the first stars formed, emitted radiation and spread newly forged elements through a young galaxy [scitechdaily.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1]. The work aims to connect galaxies observed by the James Webb Space Telescope with chemical traces preserved in ancient stars near the Milky Way [scitechdaily.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1]. The simulations begin with gas containing no heavy elements and track its chemistry and movement as the galaxy grows to roughly the Milky Way’s mass [scitechdaily.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1]. The team plans to compare more detailed models directly with telescope observations and surveys of old stars. Researchers at the University of Bath have received 40 million processor hours on UK national supercomputers for that work [scitechdaily.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1].

items.title: [Nautilus] How Sugar from Outer Space Became One of the Backbones of Life on Earth
items.content_html:
🌾 🔧 🌲 🔭 ✏️

Is there life elsewhere, or is Earth unique in the universe? This is one of humanity’s great unanswered questions.

One way to approach this mystery is to investigate how life began here on Earth. Our research explores the conditions where a mixture of molecules somehow transformed from chemistry into biology.

In a new study published in Scientific Reports, we shed new light on one possible step in this process: how a fragile sugar from outer space may have helped create the conditions for its own survival on Earth, where it eventually became the backbone of one of life’s most important molecules.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Chang’e-6 lunar soil contains a surprising magnetic time capsule
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ ✏️

Scientists studying Chang’e-6 lunar soil have discovered a previously unknown magnetic mineral in natural Moon samples: a form of metallic iron called γ-Fe. Found inside tiny impact-glass particles, the nanoscale iron can preserve a stable magnetic signal, potentially acting like a microscopic fossil of the Moon’s long-lost magnetic field.

🎨 🌾 🔧 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Ultra-detailed simulations are showing how the first stars lit up the dark Universe and seeded space with elements such as carbon, oxygen, and iron. The MEGATRON project could bridge JWST observations of the earliest galaxies with chemical clues preserved in ancient stars today.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists just made a superconductor stronger using “empty space”
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Researchers have demonstrated that quantum fluctuations in supposedly empty space can strengthen superconductivity, raising the transition temperature of an ultrathin material by as much as 5.4%. The discovery opens the possibility of using specially engineered vacuum environments to control quantum materials without direct contact or external driving.
